```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
```

SIGA (*subgroup identification based on a genetic algorithm*) looks for a
subgroup of patients with an enhanced treatment effect in a two-arm
randomised trial. This vignette walks through a complete analysis of
simulated time-to-event data. The method itself is described in
`vignette("siga-method")`.

```{r}
library(SIGA)
```

## Data

The data must contain the outcome, a treatment variable with two values and
the candidate predictors (numeric, ordered factors, factors, logical or
character). We use model B3 of the SIGA paper: 300 patients, 20 covariates,
30% censoring, and a predictive subgroup $x_4 > 1$ and $x_5 = 1$ in which the
experimental treatment reduces the hazard substantially, plus the prognostic
covariates $x_2$ and $x_9$.

```{r}
dat <- siga_simulate(300, model = "B3", seed = 2024)
dim(dat)
head(dat[, 1:8])
mean(attr(dat, "true_subgroup"))   # proportion of patients in the true subgroup
```

The model is written as `outcome ~ treatment | predictors`. The predictors
can be listed (`x1 + x2`), or `.` uses every other column (`. - id` excludes
`id`). Here `trt` is coded 0/1, so 0 is the control arm; for other codings set
`control_arm`, e.g. `control_arm = "placebo"`.

## Prescreening

`siga_screen()` shows which predictors interact with the treatment. SIGA
repeats this step inside every resample and keeps the top
$k = \lceil 20/2 \rceil = 10$ candidates.

```{r}
siga_screen(Surv(time, status) ~ trt | ., data = dat)
```

## Running SIGA

`siga()` runs the complete procedure. The defaults are the recommended
settings: `eta = 0.2` (0.25 for binary endpoints), `theta = 0.5`, 10 resamples, and a genetic algorithm
with 50 individuals, 50 generations and 5 sub-populations (`siga_control()`)
in every resample and in the final search. The analysis of 300 patients takes
about 20 seconds on one core; `n_cores` distributes the resamples over several
cores.

```{r}
fit <- siga(Surv(time, status) ~ trt | ., data = dat, eta = 0.2, theta = 0.5, seed = 1)
fit
```

The printout gives the overall hazard ratio, the mean hazard ratio of the
subgroups found in the resamples when applied to the held-out patients, the
threshold $(1 - \eta) \times$ overall hazard ratio, the selection frequency of
the predictors, and — if a subgroup is identified — its definition and the
treatment effects in the subgroup and its complement. `summary()` adds the
prescreening of the complete data, the distribution of the held-out effects
and the best subgroup of each sub-population of the final search.

```{r}
summary(fit)
```

## Plots

```{r, fig.height = 4}
plot(fit, "frequency")   # selection frequency of the predictors, with theta
plot(fit, "resamples")   # held-out hazard ratios of the resampled subgroups
```

```{r, fig.height = 4}
plot(fit, "effect")      # Kaplan-Meier curves by arm in the subgroup and complement
plot(fit, "convergence") # best objective value per generation and sub-population
```

## Other tuning parameters without recomputation

The decision rule only depends on the stored resampling results, so `update()`
changes `eta` (multiplicity control) and `theta` (complexity control) without
repeating the resampling. The result is the same as running `siga()` again
with the same seed. With 10 resamples a borderline decision can depend on the
seed, so it is worth repeating an analysis with a few seeds (see
`vignette("siga-method")`).

```{r}
update(fit, eta = 0.25, theta = 0.7)
```

## Applying the subgroup to new patients

`predict()` returns the subgroup membership and `subgroup_effect()` estimates
the treatment effects, for instance in an independent validation set:

```{r}
new <- siga_simulate(2000, model = "B3", seed = 99)
table(predicted = predict(fit, new), true = attr(new, "true_subgroup"))
subgroup_effect(fit, data = new)
```

The rule can also be used as R code, e.g. with `subset()`:

```{r}
fit$rule
format(fit$rule, style = "R")
```

## Cross-validation

`siga_cv()` estimates how well the procedure generalises by running it on
the training part of every fold and evaluating the subgroup on the held-out
fold (the paper used 100 repetitions of 5-fold cross-validation). It can also
be used to compare tuning parameters. Each fold runs a complete `siga()`, so
this is the most expensive function; use `n_cores`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
cv <- siga_cv(Surv(time, status) ~ trt | ., data = dat, k = 5, repeats = 20,
              eta = 0.2, theta = 0.5, n_cores = 8, seed = 1)
summary(cv)
```

## Genetic algorithm search only

`siga_search()` runs only the genetic algorithm on given predictors, without
prescreening and resampling. Its result is always the best subgroup of the
search and is therefore optimistic; use it for exploration.

```{r}
s <- siga_search(Surv(time, status) ~ trt | x2 + x4 + x5 + x9, data = dat, seed = 1)
s
```

## Reproducibility and parallel computing

Every resample, sub-population and cross-validation fold has its own random
number stream derived from `seed`. Results are identical for any number of
cores, and `set.seed()` before the call has the same effect as `seed`.
Parallel computing (`n_cores > 1`) starts background R processes, which
requires the package to be installed (not only loaded with `devtools`).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit4 <- siga(Surv(time, status) ~ trt | ., data = dat, seed = 1, n_cores = 4)
identical(fit4$resamples, fit$resamples)   # TRUE
```
